name: Madhubani
description: Intricate, densely filled folk paintings of deities, nature and ritual scenes.
history: Originating in the Mithila region, it was traditionally painted by women on freshly plastered walls for weddings and festivals. It reached wider audiences after 1934 when paper paintings were documented.
significance: A women-led tradition that records ritual, marriage and nature symbolism, now a GI-tagged craft.
characteristics: Fish, peacocks, sun and lotus motifs
No empty space; patterns fill the frame
techniques: Line drawing first, colour fill second
facts: Also called Mithila painting.
Bharni, Kachni and Godna are classic styles.

name: Warli
description: Minimal white drawings of circles, triangles and squares depicting village life.
history: Practised by the Warli tribe of the Sahyadri range, originally on mud walls of huts during harvest and weddings.
significance: Expresses a community's bond with nature and the cycle of farming and celebration.
facts: The sun and moon are drawn as circles.
Chowk is the central ritual motif.

name: Kalamkari
description: Hand-painted or block-printed cotton textiles with epics and floral vines.
history: Named from 'kalam' (pen) and 'kari' (craft). Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam styles flourished under Golconda and Vijayanagara patronage.
significance: Preserves mythological storytelling and natural dye knowledge on fabric.
techniques: Cloth treated with milk and myrobalan
facts: Srikalahasti style is freehand; Machilipatnam uses blocks.
Around 17 steps are needed per cloth.

name: Pattachitra
description: Cloth-based scroll paintings with bold outlines telling Jagannath and Puranic tales.
history: Linked to the Jagannath temple at Puri, painted by chitrakars for centuries.
significance: Central to temple rituals and storytelling traditions.
facts: 'Patta' means cloth, 'chitra' picture.
Brush hair comes from animal fur.

name: Gond Art
description: Vivid animals and trees filled with dots, dashes and flowing lines.
history: Painted by the Gond people, historically on floors and walls; Jangarh Singh Shyam brought it to canvas in the 1980s.
significance: Expresses the belief that every being carries a spirit.
facts: 'Digna' floor patterns are its roots.
Seen as a way to bring good luck.

name: Tanjore Painting
description: Rich devotional panels with gold foil, gems and rounded divine figures.
history: Flourished under Thanjavur Nayaks and Marathas from the 16th century.
significance: Devotional art for homes and temples; GI-tagged.
facts: Also called Thanjavur painting.
Jackwood is often used for the base.

name: Phad Painting
description: Long cloth scrolls narrating the epics of folk heroes like Pabuji and Devnarayan.
history: Painted by Joshi families of Bhilwara for bhopa priest-singers who perform before the scroll.
significance: A portable temple used in oral performance traditions.
facts: A scroll may be 15 feet long.
Shahpura and Bhilwara are its traditional centres.

name: Cheriyal Painting
description: Vibrant red-dominant scrolls with village and epic scenes in comic-strip panels.
history: Made by Nakashi families in Cheriyal to accompany storytelling by the Kaki Padagollu community.
significance: Visual accompaniment to caste-specific oral epics.
facts: GI-tagged in 2007.
Scrolls are read like a film reel.

name: Kerala Mural
description: Temple wall paintings of deities in rich earth colours with sculptural features.
history: Flourished from the 9th to 12th century in temples and palaces such as Mattancherry.
significance: Expresses Hindu mythology with a strict canonical colour code.
facts: Green base (pacha) is typical.
Follows texts on colour and iconography.

name: Mandana Art
description: White geometric designs on red ochre floors and walls for festivals.
history: A folk practice of rural communities to invite prosperity, refreshed at each festival.
significance: Protective ritual art made by women for Diwali and weddings.
facts: Drawn fresh each festival season.
Symmetry is central to designs.
